title: Chapter 11: A Drawer Full of Tomorrow
content: The copier jams on packet twenty-two, which is Nadine Cotter, which feels personal.

Wren opens the front door of the machine and the tray comes out with her, and there is a page folded into the roller like a bad hand of cards. Ruthie Pyle watches from behind the counter with a spatula in her fist.
"You are feeding it wrong," Ruthie says.
"I am feeding it the same way I fed the first twenty-one."
"Then it is tired." Ruthie turns back to the grill. "So am I. It is six forty in the morning and you have been in my dining room since five."
Wren smooths the page. Form 9, page two, section 6: cause, as certified. She has written drowned forty-one times this week in the same block letters, and the word has stopped looking like a word.

Four tables pushed together. Forty-one stacks, each one clipped with a binder clip from the hardware store. Three pages of Form 9 and one page of the log, and the log page is the part that matters, because the log page is the part with the name on it.

For Anna Voss Rusk she chose 4 August 2003, the day she crossed as a child with her mother, nine souls, fare paid. For Deacon Ross she chose the four hundred and sixth crossing, out of spite. For Owen Pike she chose 14 May 1994, 6:12 a.m., one soul, eight minutes before the gate opened for silt, and the pencil in the margin.

Forty-one is not a number she picked for drama. One file is a favor a clerk can lose. Forty-one files have to be taken in the order they are received, and a stack that size cannot disappear without somebody being able to prove it was there, because every one of them gets a receipt, and a receipt is a stub in a book the county keeps whether it wants to or not.

She printed the log pages at the county library on Tuesday, fifteen cents a sheet. The librarian watched her feed the machine for forty minutes and then said, without looking up, "You want the date stamps darker," and went back to her desk.
Ruthie comes over with the coffee pot and fills the cup Wren has not touched.
"You are going to break my machine."
"I will pay for the toner."

"You will pay for the toner and you will eat something." Ruthie sets a plate down. Toast, cut in triangles, the way she cuts it for children and for men who have been up all night. "Eat. Then fix the machine."

At eight ten Wren stacks the finished packets in a milk crate, forty-one of them, and walks up Third Street with the crate against her hip. The morning is cold in the way October mornings are cold here, all surface, no weight.
The Annex opens at eight thirty. She is there at eight forty and the queue is already nine people.
By nine it is twenty. By ten it is out the door and down the steps.
The window has a bell on it. Wren rings it at 9:02 with the crate on the counter, and Hollis Drane comes out of the back with his cardigan buttoned wrong and his reading glasses on a cord.
"Miss Aubrey."
"Forty-one filings." She sets the first stack down. "Form 9, with underlying record attached."
Hollis looks at the crate the way a man looks at weather coming across a field.
"You cannot file forty-one."
"Show me the rule."

He does not show her the rule, because there is no rule. There is a fee schedule, and the fee schedule says nine dollars a filing. Wren opens the coffee can she has been carrying inside the crate and counts out three hundred and sixty-nine dollars in ones and fives on the counter, in stacks of ten, with nine in the last stack, and Hollis has to count it twice because the window does not take cash after ten and it is not ten yet.

The money is the last two weeks of ferry fares, taken before the cable housing was cut and after, in the dark, from people who put bills in a coffee can and did not ask for change. She knows most of their faces. She could not tell you one of their names without the log.
Then he gets to the box.
Section 4. Relationship to decedent. He taps it with the cap of his pen.
"You are not kin to these people."
"No."
"Then you cannot sign it."
Wren takes the pen out of his hand, which is a thing she has never done, and writes in the box in block letters, one word.
CARRIER.
Hollis reads it. He reads it again. Something in his face does an honest day's work.
"That is not a relationship."
"It is on the river."

He looks at the queue behind her, which is now thirty people and one man with a fence permit who has been waiting since eight. He looks at the crate. He looks at the clock, and the clock is the only thing in the room that has never lied to him.
Then he picks up the stamp.
The first one lands on Owen Pike at 9:14 a.m. The sound is small and wet and final, and Wren feels it in her back teeth. RECEIVED, 1 OCT 2026, DISTRICT 4.
"Receipt," she says.
"I have to write them by hand."
"Then write them by hand."

He writes them by hand. Carbon paper, triplicate, a ballpoint that skips. Number 77120 through 77160, one for every filing, and his handwriting gets worse around the nineteenth because his hand has started to shake and he is pretending it has not.

Wren stacks the yellow copies in the lid of the crate and does not look at the queue, because if she looks at the queue she will start counting it, and counting is the only thing that has ever made her feel like crying.
At 10:20 she steps outside for air. A woman in a green coat stands at the foot of the steps with a shopping bag against her leg, not in the line, just watching it.
"Which one is Vernon," the woman says.
"File nineteen," Wren says. "Vernon Ash. He crossed on a Tuesday in April 2007 with a bag of seed corn. The fare was waived."
The woman's mouth opens. She does not cry the way people cry in films. She puts her hand flat on the shopping bag and holds it there.
"He always carried that corn," she says. "I told him it would get wet."
"It got wet," Wren says. "He put it under the bench."
That is true, because it is in the margin.
At eleven the line reaches the street. The photographer from the county paper comes up the steps sideways with a bag bigger than his shoulders and asks Hollis if he can shoot inside.
"No," Hollis says.
The kid shoots through the glass door, flash on, and the flash makes everybody in the line turn at once, forty faces in a lit window, which is the picture that runs on Sunday.
Then he points the camera at Wren and asks her name.
"You know my name," she says. "You put it in the paper."
"I know it. I still have to ask." He flips the notebook open. "It is the only rule I have."
She gives him the name. He writes it in a notebook with a golf pencil and underlines Aubrey twice.
At eleven thirty Ruthie arrives with a box of coffee and a stack of paper cups and stands at the back of the line.
"You do not have to stand in line," Wren says.
"I know," Ruthie says. "That is why."

The man with the fence permit gets to the window at 11:50 and Wren lets him go, and then she lets the woman with the dog license go, and then a man with a shed, and Hollis watches her do it and says nothing, because he is beginning to understand that she is not going to be rude and it is going to be much worse for him than rudeness.

Behind her the fence permit man is telling the woman with the dog license that he has been coming to this window for thirty years and has never seen one person file more than two things in a day. He says it loudly. He says it to be heard. Wren does not turn around. By two o'clock he will be telling it in the diner instead, which is better.
At 12:40 there are nine packets left. At 1:30 there are two.

Somewhere around the twentieth filing Hollis stopped saying that this was unusual. Around the thirtieth he stopped sighing. Now he works with the flat rhythm of a man who has decided that the day is going to happen to him and there is no point in arguing with the day.

The last one is Elias Aubrey. She put him last on purpose. She filed him once already, on the fourteenth of September, with a pen hovering over section 6 and a clerk saying a sentence. This time she has four pages. Form 9, three pages, and the underlying record is the page from 12 September, nine souls, and the water column with +6 and 9:47 in her own pencil.
Hollis reads it. His mouth does something.
"I knew him," he says.
"Everybody knew him."
"I mean I liked him." He stamps the page. The sound is the same as all the others. "This one is going to be a problem."
"They are all going to be a problem."
"No." Hollis shakes his head slowly. "This one has a name on it that people say out loud."
He writes the receipt. Number 77160. Then he puts the pen down and looks at the drawer, the second desk, bottom left, and for one second his hand moves toward it and stops.

Wren puts the slip with the others and squares the stack. Forty-one yellow copies, in order, 77120 through 77160. It is the first thing the Authority has given her in nineteen days with a date on it that she did not have to write in herself.
"These will be reviewed," he says. "In order."
Wren takes the yellow copy and says nothing, because there is nothing that would make the sentence smaller than it is.

Her right hand has a cramp in the meat below the thumb. She has not written this much since school. The word has started to look like a shape instead of a thing, so she says it in her head, once, to keep it a thing. Drowned.
She is at the door with the empty crate when the phone on Hollis's desk rings.
He answers it the way he answers everything, softly, with his name. Then his back changes. It straightens, and his free hand goes to the knot of his tie, which he is not wearing.
"Yes, Director," he says.
Wren stops with her hand on the door.
Hollis listens for a long time. He says yes twice more. Then he covers the mouthpiece with his palm, and his face is the face of a man holding a hot dish with no cloth.
"She wants the person who filed them," he says, and holds out the receiver.
highlight: Wren files forty-one forms in a morning, jams the copier, and the director demands the person who filed them.
